title: dfilter: Allow bytestrings that are also protocol names on RHS
description:
Protocol names can only be on the left hand side of filter expressions.
If a protocol name with an even number of characters ("fc", "dc", "ff",
"fefd", etc.) is on the right hand side of a filter expressions and
can be interpreted as a byte string instead, do so.  Fix #12810.

I don't get this change. We now support doing `contains` and `matches` for strings matching a protocol name with hex digits, but we still don't support using other strings which happens to match a protocol (without using quotes).

Example: We support `tcp contains dna` but not `tcp contains dns`.

I think it's still difficult to understand this difference, and it's not clear that the user must use quotes in some cases.

Since protocols are not valid in the RHS of `contains`, the question is what should `fc` (for example) represent in the RHS other than a protocol. Whether it matches a field or not need not really factor into the question, right?

> Example: We support `tcp contains dna` but not `tcp contains dns`.

Not ideal, I agree, we should support neither or both, but that is related to the problem I alluded to with assuming something that matches a protocol name *is* in fact always a protocol name (unless there is an exception like the one this change introduces).

More over I think we should not support `tcp contains dna`, only `tcp contains "dna"`. It would be better to reject unquoted strings (but probably too late for that).

`contains` is tricky because it matches all strings, but bytearrays are used on the right side for range comparisons, etc.

I find having to quote ordinary strings for `contains` and `matches` not so bad, but having to quote byte arrays as `mpt2[2] == "\xff"` more annoying. (Though `mp2t[2] == FF` was always allowed, if not `mp2t[2] == ff` even though `mp2t[1] = fe` would be fine.)

It would be possible to get rid of the "is it a byte array" test and re-interpret _any_ protocol name on the right hand side as unparsed, so as to allow `tcp contains dns`, but I think I agree that the problem is that unquoted regular strings are allowed (but too late to change that.)

That already makes the `contains` operator have unexpected behavior in that if the RHS is can be interpreted as a byte array it does that, but if not it allows it to be an unquoted string.

That means that `frame contains Id` matches a frame with the bytes `\x49 \x64` in it (same as `frame contains "Id"`, but `frame contains dF` does *not* match a frame with `\x64 \x46` as `frame contains "dF"` does but matches a frame with `\xdf`, same as `frame contains df`.) (Seen in [this file](/uploads/52ef3170c87fa799df85b1deab5181ab/pbm_p1_sample.pcapng) with frames 1 and 6.)
resolved all threads

I think it's more useful (and easier to do consistently) to allow unquoted byte arrays, but trickier to allow unquoted strings, given that there's already confusion with `contains` and `matches` about whether an unquoted literal on the RHS is a literal byte array or a literal string.

There is confusion because the syntax for arrays and strings (and protocol names) is ambiguous.

Under the circumstance I think the best possible heuristic for `contains` to parse a sequence of characters on the RHS is: try to parse a byte array, then try to parse an unquoted string, then error out. No concern needs to be given for protocol names (on the RHS).

So we could do that by changing it to just reinterpret any protocol on the right side as unparsed, whether it parses as a byte array or not, and then `contains` will do exactly that. (It seems like something that could be more cleanly done in the grammar rather than the semantics eventually.)

I can do another merge request for that.

@johnthacker Yeah, I agree. I also think it should be fixed at the lexical level but if you want to implement that first I believe it would be a massive improvement and may be simpler to backport.

I'll hold off on working on this then so we don't duplicate effort.

> Under the circumstance I think the best possible heuristic for `contains` to parse a sequence of characters on the RHS is: try to parse a byte array, then try to parse an unquoted string, then error out. No concern needs to be given for protocol names (on the RHS).

Is this really always the best heuristic? `fz` is the string "fz" but `fc` is the octet 0xfc? Not very intuitive. Maybe strings need some special-casing, like not a valid unquoted string if less than three chars. Within the constraint of backward compatibility there is a little room to work with but it requires some investigation of the current reality.

> Yeah, I agree. I also think it should be fixed at the lexical level but if you want to implement that first I believe it would be a massive improvement and may be simpler to backport

Done in !4313.

The type rules are much more complicated than I thought so anything like !4313 is almost guaranteed to change some part of the language behaviour not covered in the test suite. Back to the drawing board.


I personally lean towards af3885bcf160d80c515ca6b71479ca9faabb45df being a mistake. I don't think we should maintain a moving target of guessing what the user "probably" means and changing the semantics. Guaranteed it will be wrong sometimes and there are so many more quirks in the language. It becomes even more surprising with these exceptions. If this practice is generalized then the only way to understand how the language works is to study the source code.

> If this practice is generalized then the only way to understand how the language works is to study the source code.

Yes, I agree. I also think it would be useful to update the [User Guide](https://www.wireshark.org/docs/wsug_html/#_display_filter_fields), which is fairly incomplete when it comes to describing the filter language. I have a separate merge request !4323 which adds a description of how the absolute time fields work (which is not necessarily as expected; for example, even fields always displayed as UTC must be filtered in local time.)

The User Guide doesn't explain byte strings in general, only gives some idea of how they work for `FT_ETHER`. Optimally every ftype would have a brief entry. (Well, almost all, at this point not clear that `FT_VINES` or `FT_IPXNET` need to be called out.)

Commit a975d478badf9e3cf1e5faa894197eb27b26fc41 removed the issue of protocols on the RHS for "matches". Regular expressions are text strings, not unparsed values.

I'm still not sure what should be done for the remaining cases, if anything. As noted before the ambiguity of byte arrays and variables is inherent to the syntax. The first step is to document in detail the heuristic to parse this, I think.

> The User Guide doesn't explain byte strings in general, only gives some idea of how they work for `FT_ETHER`. Optimally every ftype would have a brief entry. (Well, almost all, at this point not clear that `FT_VINES` or `FT_IPXNET` need to be called out.)

Good points.
A separate but related issue is to make FT_PROTOCOL and FT_BYTES more compatible.
